conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I’m Dr. Reyes. You’re in the hospital because you came in with chest pain after being punched near your defibrillator. We’re going to figure out what’s going on. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hurting here, right over the device. It’s tender when I move or breathe deep. And I’ve been nauseous, throwing up a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned the device fired four times? We checked with electrophysiology, and the device didn’t actually fire. There’s no record of shocks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, really? I felt something—like jolts. But maybe it was just the punch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The trauma could definitely cause that sensation. We did a chest X-ray, and there’s no fracture or damage to the device. Your heart rhythm is irregular, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… but I also have pain in my upper right belly and I’ve been dizzy for about two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You had a fall recently with a head strike? Your CT head was normal, so we’re not worried about a brain injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I slipped. But the dizziness hasn’t gone away. And the headaches are bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those could be related to alcohol withdrawal. Your blood alcohol level was very high—323—when you arrived. That’s severe intoxication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had two pints earlier that day. But I didn’t think it was that bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, especially with your heart condition. We’re monitoring you for withdrawal symptoms. We’ve started you on vitamins and a medication called diazepam to help prevent seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been shaky and sweating. Is that part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are classic signs. We’re scoring your symptoms regularly. You’ve needed a few doses because you scored high on the scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay? I don’t want to have a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not showing signs of serious withdrawal so far. No hallucinations or confusion. We’re giving you medication to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve got some test results. Your liver enzymes are elevated—AST is higher than ALT—which suggests recent heavy drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean my liver is damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely alcohol-induced injury, but not permanent if you stop drinking. Your ultrasound showed no gallstones or liver disease. We also saw some old rib fractures on the X-ray—probably from past trauma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember breaking ribs. But I’ve had rough times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re healing. But back to your belly pain and nausea—we think it’s from alcohol use and gastritis. We’ve increased your omeprazole and added anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Last time, I was putting food in my vomit bin. I was confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was noted in your last admission. We’re watching closely. Your heart function is still weak—EF around 25%—but stable. No signs of heart failure worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart enzymes twice—both negative. No heart attack. EKG shows old damage but no new changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I took eight nitroglycerin pills. Was that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. It can cause headaches and low blood pressure. But it didn’t help, which makes us think the pain isn’t from heart ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the chest pain is just from the punch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. There’s tenderness over the device pocket, but no infection or fluid collection. We’ll keep it clean and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low potassium and magnesium. That’s common with vomiting and your diuretic. We’re giving supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take potassium at home. But I haven’t been regular with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We repleted it. You also had a short run of fast heartbeats on the monitor—8 beats—but it stopped on its own. Likely due to low electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It was brief and asymptomatic. We’re correcting the levels to prevent more episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bilirubin is high—mostly indirect. But ultrasound is normal, and you’re not anemic. This looks like Gilbert’s syndrome, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not liver failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It’s a mild genetic condition. It can flare with fasting or illness, like now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. Your tremors are gone, and you haven’t vomited. We’re stopping the withdrawal meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. What about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge today. Continue all your heart meds—especially dabigatran for stroke prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should improve. Use acetaminophen if needed. Avoid alcohol completely—it’s dangerous with your heart and liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need to stop. It’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can connect you with support services. Your health depends on it. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Stay safe and take care of yourself.
